reviews.text: Hexadel ended up surprising me in a really good way. The first thing that stood out was the UI: every dropdown, new text option, or menu comes in with this simple, old-school animation that gives the game a playful, almost childlike feel. It is minimal but unique, and even things like dragging bars in the menus feel charming rather than generic. The music matches that vibe perfectly. It is very old school and simple, something you can genuinely leave on in the background while working or even falling asleep, and it never really becomes annoying or overbearing. ​ Gameplay and Mechanics Underneath the simple presentation, the core gameplay is much deeper than it first appears. In the campaign, you start at level 1 and climb up as you win, but if your main building loses all its health, you die and the entire campaign resets, sending you right back to level 1. Every level is made up of multiple waves. At the start of each wave, time pauses and you can buy defense parts with the money you earned from killing enemies in the previous wave. Sometimes there are special offers on this purchase screen, and if you want a different defence, you can reroll the selection, which is a nice bit of quality-of-life. After the first wave, things no longer stay paused, so you are adding defenses while enemies are moving and attacking, which keeps the pressure on. The game gives you both automated and manual tools to handle this. You have towers that shoot on their own, but they need ammo supplied via conveyors connected to your main base, so you have to think carefully about how you route those conveyors to keep everything stocked. You can even stack up to three towers in one slot at different heights to increase range and coverage. On top of that, there are walls and traps that let you slow enemies, giving you or your towers more time to finish them off. The catch is that you always have to protect your main building’s health; once it is hit enough times, the run is over and you are back to the start. There is also a manual shooting mechanic that adds another layer to the strategy. You cannot just tap rapidly to fire; you have to tap and hold to charge, then release to fire multiple bullets at once, followed by a cooldown period. This makes it important to set up your defenses properly and then decide when it is worth using your manual shots to cover weak spots your towers are not facing. Later on, you start unlocking small boosts during progression, like extra health for your walls, which feels rewarding and helps your builds evolve over time. ​ Learning Curve and Difficulty The learning curve is definitely on the steeper side, especially at the start. The tutorial is super confusing the first time through. There is a moment where the game asks you to “Sell a building/tower,” and it is not at all clear that you are supposed to tap the big X icon and then tap the building itself. Nothing is written below the icons to explain what they do, so you end up clicking around until it finally makes sense. The game does show you the controls every time you load into the game, but there is no “Controls” option in the main menu or when you hit escape to pause, which would really help when you need a reminder later (while in a level). That said, if you run the tutorial twice and then jump into the campaign, things start to connect. It took around 30 minutes before the core mechanics really clicked for me, and after a few more rounds, I finally felt like I understood “how to play” instead of just reacting. Level 5 in particular is crazy difficult and will probably knock you back to level 1 more than once. After about two hours, you will likely have replayed levels 1–4 multiple times, but that repetition is where the strategy part really sinks in. You start thinking carefully about where to place towers, where to drop traps and walls, when to manually shoot, and when to just let your towers handle things. At that point, it becomes properly fun and satisfying rather than confusing. ​ One small annoyance is that when you die and have to restart, you see the same dialogues again every single time. It is not a deal-breaker, but after multiple restarts it does get a bit tiring and makes you wish for a “skip dialogue” option completely but there's a "skip per dialogue" option when you hit "space" bar. ​ UI, Audio, and Performance On the technical side, the game runs really well. On a Ryzen 5 5600x paired with an RX 6750 XT, there were no crashes, no noticeable stutters, and no FPS drops during the playthrough, even as the waves got busier. The graphics options are very simple, but for this kind of minimalist game, that is more than enough. It feels properly optimized for what it is trying to do. ​ The audio is mostly solid, especially the chill, old-school soundtrack that fits the minimalist style nicely. There is, however, a small bug in the audio settings: turning the music and UI sliders down to zero does not completely mute the music until you also turn down the master volume. It is a minor issue and not game-breaking, but still worth noting. In the shop or purchase menu, there were a few moments where it looked like there was enough money to buy something, but the game would not let the purchase go through. It seems like this might happen when your inventory or capacity is full, but the game never tells you that. A simple popup saying something like “Inventory full” would make that much clearer. On the control side, one tweak that would help is making the crosshair move a bit faster. When things get hectic, being able to aim and adjust your shots more quickly would make manual shooting feel more responsive and satisfying. ​ Final Thoughts Overall, Hexadel looks simple on the surface but hides a surprisingly deep and strategic tower defense experience. The first impression can be a bit confusing, especially with the tutorial and lack of clearly labeled icons and in-menu controls, but if you give it some time, everything starts to fall into place. Once it clicks, planning your conveyors, stacking towers, placing traps and walls, and timing your charged shots becomes genuinely engaging, and the difficulty makes each clear feel earned. If you enjoy tower defense games that are a bit unforgiving at first but reward you for sticking with them and learning their systems, Hexadel is absolutely worth checking out.

A unique and addictive tactical gem! As a fan of deckbuilders and strategy games, I found HEXADEL to be a breath of fresh air. It takes the classic card-battler formula and adds a deep layer of "Spatial Strategy" with its hexagonal grid system. The reasons I recommend it: • Brilliant Mechanics: Unlike many games where you just play cards, here, positioning is everything. Placing a trap or a conveyor in the right hex feels incredibly satisfying and rewards smart thinking. • Atmospheric Visuals: The dark, minimalist aesthetic is beautiful and helps you stay focused on the tactical puzzle at hand. It has a very cool, "gothic tech" vibe. • Addictive Loop: The challenge is real! It’s one of those games where you say "just one more run" and before you know it, an hour has passed. • Performance: The game runs very smoothly and feels stable even on my laptop. It’s clear the developer has put a lot of heart into the core gameplay. If you're looking for a strategy game that challenges your brain and offers something different from the standard genre, give HEXADEL a try. It’s polished, tactical, and very rewarding once you find the right synergies.Highly recommended for strategy and roguelike enthusiasts!

The light, jazzy atmospheric music and stark, minimalist aesthetic create a mood that's distinct but hard to express in words. It's serene, but with an underlying intensity. The gameplay has depth, both figuratively and literally, since you can build on three layers. You can tilt the vantage point, which is not only useful but also looks really cool. Difficulty-wise, it starts off easy but ramps up fast. Before you know it, you're beset with a barrage of attacks like Lucy in the Chocolate Factory! (Legends will get that reference. 😉) I'm still trying to find the best type of setup that gives the turret enough time to hold back the onslaught. Wish me luck! 💪

HEXADEL, developed and published by Planetary Gears, is a minimalist strategy experience that blends tower defense fundamentals with logistical puzzle design and base-building creativity. Framed around constructing and defending layered citadels known as “Hexadels,” the game introduces players to a neon-lit battlefield where careful planning, resource routing, and structural design matter just as much as raw defensive power. While modest in scope, it distinguishes itself through its emphasis on system interaction and emergent gameplay rather than sheer content volume. At its core, HEXADEL revolves around constructing defensive layouts to repel waves of hostile forces. Unlike traditional tower defense games that rely on predetermined paths, the structure here is more open-ended. Players design their citadel from modular components, placing walls, turrets, traps, and conveyor systems in configurations that shape how enemies are funneled and how resources circulate. The conveyor mechanics are especially central to the experience. They ensure that ammunition, power, or defensive elements are transported efficiently throughout the structure, creating a logistical layer that elevates the gameplay beyond simple turret placement. This fusion of base-building and supply management transforms each session into a dynamic puzzle of flow and balance. Strategic depth emerges gradually as systems begin interacting in unexpected ways. A well-placed conveyor may enhance a turret’s effectiveness, while poor routing can cause bottlenecks that weaken otherwise solid defenses. The player must consider not only immediate threats but also the sustainability of their layout over time. Because each Hexadel is essentially a self-designed fortress, experimentation becomes key. Some layouts emphasize tight choke points with concentrated firepower, while others prioritize distributed defenses supported by efficient resource loops. This flexibility encourages creativity and makes each defense scenario feel personal. Visually, HEXADEL embraces a sleek neon aesthetic that enhances clarity and atmosphere simultaneously. The glowing outlines of structures and enemies contrast sharply against darker backgrounds, ensuring readability even during intense moments. The minimalist art style avoids clutter, keeping the focus on structural geometry and movement patterns. Complementing this visual direction is a subdued electronic soundtrack that reinforces a thoughtful, almost meditative tone. Rather than pushing frantic energy, the presentation encourages deliberate construction and careful observation. As an evolving project, HEXADEL reflects its independent development roots. Some systems may feel lightweight or still in refinement, and the content breadth is relatively focused compared to large-scale strategy titles. However, this tight scope also means that the core mechanics receive clear attention. The game prioritizes polish within its foundational systems rather than overwhelming players with excessive features. For strategy enthusiasts who appreciate iterative experimentation and streamlined mechanics, this design philosophy can be particularly appealing. Replayability stems largely from self-driven experimentation and optimization. Because layouts are player-created, there is inherent variability in how each session unfolds. The desire to refine defensive efficiency or attempt new structural concepts can sustain engagement even in the absence of expansive campaign narratives. Leaderboards and progression elements further encourage players to improve performance metrics and explore alternative tactical approaches. Ultimately, HEXADEL stands as a thoughtful hybrid of tower defense and logistical puzzle design. It offers a focused experience built around creative fortification and strategic resource management within a clean, futuristic aesthetic. While it may not offer the breadth of a full-scale strategy epic, it compensates with emergent depth and design flexibility. For players drawn to methodical planning, system interaction, and the satisfaction of constructing an efficient defensive network from the ground up, HEXADEL delivers a compact yet engaging strategic challenge. Rating: 5/10

Really unique, simple and fun tower defense with neon light only. It might be a little struggle at the first but when you know and more familiar with the gameplay, it's really easy to learn and really fun with the puzzle part. The music is really relaxing too when playing this game.

This game is a blend of tower defense and puzzle, with a really great strategic element. The genres are very well interwoven, the overall design is good, it's aesthetically pleasing, and the music is incredibly relaxing. A very good experience, highly recommended even in early access. I can't wait for the full release!
It starts simple but quickly makes you think about space, timing, and structure placement. Enjoyable and worth playing.
A small but engaging strategy experience that’s easy to pick up and satisfying to figure out.
Bright neon lights and clever puzzles make this a perfect chill zone where building your dream citadel feels like high-stakes Lego fun outsmarting ghosts has never been cooler
A stylish, neon-drenched layered tower defense puzzle game. Build complex citadels, manage dynamic conveyors, and outsmart the machine in this chill, minimalist strategy experience. Truly unique!
This is pretty different to your standard tower defence experience. There's some annoying complexity to having different layers to build on. You also need to manual target enemies all the time.
A stylish retro-inspired shooter with fast action and neon-soaked visuals. HEXADEL delivers satisfying arcade gameplay that keeps you coming back.
